en: Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty, recorded by his disciple Guanding:
Regarding "Superior Knowledge and Vision," this mind is superior to form and is not bound by form; the mind is able to transform [it].
Because it is form,
it is called "superior knowledge.
As for "superior vision":
Since they have attained mastery over their own minds regarding purity, impurity, and so forth,
and have achieved realization through contemplation,
it is called "superior vision."
These two are subsumed under the second dhyāna.
When the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) are accomplished, one does not even spare one's own body,
let alone material wealth or the bodies of others.
The sages of antiquity who abdicated their thrones and yielded their kingdoms, and those who returned their oxen and washed their ears in the stream—
all were people of former lives who had practiced this contemplation until it became their natural disposition, free from further attachment or defilement.
If one does not grasp this meaning, one will crave it until death;
how then could one suddenly abandon glory and renounce one's position?
The latter four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are accomplished within the fourth dhyāna.
In the third dhyāna, the bliss is so abundant that it cannot be transformed;
this is what is said according to the Śrāvaka-dharma.
In the Bodhisattva-dharma, however, each dhyāna is transformed by the next.
How could they not exist?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that blue, yellow, red,
and white derive from real dharmas (*dravyadharma*).
The *Yingluo* (Adornment) Sūtra states: "Earth, water, fire, and wind are derived from provisional names;
they mutually encompass one another.
Within these four bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), all internal and external forms are exhausted, leaving only eight colors."
There is only a transformation of quantity;
there is no transformation of quality, whether good or bad.
The ten universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) are contained within the fourth dhyāna.
In the first dhyāna, applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra) are predominant;
in the second dhyāna, joy (prīti) is active;
in the third dhyāna, bliss (sukha) is active.
It cannot pervade all places universally;
only by means of unwavering mindfulness and wisdom can one achieve universal pervasion.
By means of blue, one pervades the ten directions, such that the ten directions are entirely blue.
The same applies to the other colors;
therefore, they are called "all-pervasive bases" (*sarvatraga*).
If one enters into the "all-base" (*sarvāyatana*) by means of blue, then at all times yellow comes to enter into that blue.
They also pervade all places;
the fundamental characteristics of blue and yellow are not lost as they interpenetrate,
yet they do not become confused with one another.
The same applies to the other colored bases.
These are called the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities).
This consists of emitting color from within the mind so that it pervades all places.
How could that which depends on external tree leaves as its condition pervade all places?
If the internal mind cannot be stabilized, how can it transform external tree leaves?
One must first be able to transform the mind before one can transform the leaves.
Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s citation of the blue lotus (*utpala*),
it employs an external metaphor to illustrate an internal point for fear that others might not understand;
one must not, however, cling to the metaphor as the definitive meaning itself.
If one practices the clear observation (vibhūta-vipaśyanā) internally without the skeletal person (*aṭṭhika-puggala*) and does not release the eight colors,
then when cultivating the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), one should rely on external conditions;
perhaps this is indeed how it should be.
Within those who do not destroy the Dharma, one may be self-reliant and need not depend on others.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva cultivates the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and possesses various practices,
if they do not penetrate the distinction between the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-āśrita*), greed and stinginess may arise.
If this contemplation is clear,
one would wish to relinquish even one's own body;
how much less would one begrudge one's own possessions while coveting the wealth of others?
This is what is called *dāna*.
Having attained such a contemplation, one does not violate the precepts for the sake of wealth or sensual pleasure,
nor does one harm the owner of that wealth to bring the goods back to oneself.
To seek complete success through a hundred forms of deception is absolutely impossible;
such a person is merely a hollow title.
When one attains this contemplation, even if others touch, disturb, or plunder one,
one never gives rise to anger or contention; regarding such filth and excrement as nothing more than refuse—
this is called patience.
When this contemplation is perfected, one does not rely on the impure corpse-body,
nor does one allow the concentrated mind to regress amidst an impure land;
this is called diligence.
This contemplation is capable of fully encompassing the cultivation through observation,
the exercise of supernormal powers and transformations,
and the knowledge of vows, the crown-protrusion, and so forth.
This is called dhyāna; when this contemplation is attained, all phenomena—both subject and object—are found to be unattainable.
Being neither arising nor ceasing, they are ultimately pure.
This is called prajñā.
All dharma-gates of the concentration of all paths are transformed and accomplished within the superior stations; with mastery over mental concentration, one revolves, departs, and abides at will.
One performs all dharma-gates, which are accomplished immediately according to the mind.
Just as a swift horse breaks through an array while maintaining self-control,
at that time the mind becomes luminous and pure, and no further demonic activities arise.
The mind masters the demons, and the demons cannot destroy the mind.
If those who practice the four samādhis attain this Dharma,
they will for the most part advance into the stage of the five grades of disciples. Why is this so?
The power of these aids to the path is great, enabling one to swiftly approach the Pool of Coolness.
Up to this point is the arousal of the dhyāna of contemplation;
it is also the manifestation of the signs of Mahāyāna dhyāna.
If one has not yet refined and cultivated [the mind], even an ordinary person cannot attain the state of "non-arising" (an-utpāda) to be discussed;
as for those who have produced it separately according to the sutras and śāstras, there is no need to speak further.
○ Seventh, regarding the manifestation of a compassionate mind: compassion is the fundamental basis, as explained extensively in the preceding and following sections.
Suddenly, taking as an object the aspect of happiness belonging to all sentient beings—
free from enmity and affliction, gladdening the heart and pleasing the mind—
he may see them attaining the happiness of humans or see them attaining the happiness of the heavens.
Through skillful cultivation, one attains the concentration of liberation, and the mind becomes clear and distinct;
there is not a single sentient being who does not obtain happiness.
Initially, one treads step by step through subtle tranquility, and subsequently enters ever-deeper meditative absorption; however, there are only three types of objects of focus.
If one attains happiness by taking relatives as the object, it is called "extensive"; if one takes neutral persons as the object, it is called "great";
and if one takes enemies as the object, it is called "immeasurable."
Furthermore, when sentient beings in one direction attain happiness, it is called "vast";
in the four intermediate directions, it is called "great";
and in the ten directions, it is called "immeasurable."
This concentration is of two kinds: obscured and unobscured.
If the mind takes sentient beings as its object, it definitely produces the perception of happiness, and the mind becomes extremely clear.
Yet, regarding the object of focus, one does not see sentient beings obtaining happiness;
this is when it is non-obscured internally but obscured externally.
Furthermore, there is the case where the internal mind is bright and pure, while externally one sees the attainment of happiness.
This is what is meant by being neither obscured internally nor externally.
If one first attains this meditative concentration and subsequently manifests the fivefold qualities,
sentient beings will first perceive that they have all attained happiness.
When the mind is united with concentration, one’s own mind is also joyful;
having attained liberation through skillful cultivation,
this is called a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
Through discernment, one attains happiness;
or rather, one clearly understands the immeasurable gradations among humans and celestial beings.
This is called the branch of contemplation: regarding enemies and kin as equal, one no longer fears enemies nor suffers from anxiety for kin.
It is called the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*).
When the factor of joy moves and the mind and spirit are refreshed and delighted, it is also like the characteristic of obtaining bliss (*sukha*) from its object;
this is called the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*).
When the meditative state becomes increasingly profound and the mind is maintained without wavering,
it is called the factor of one-pointedness (*ekāgratā*).
This is termed "identical to the root" (*mūlasamāna*), yet its flavor (*dharmarasa*) is eternally distinct.
Just as molasses, honey, and water have the same flavor when cold but differ when heated,
so too, if one generates only the fundamental [dhyāna] and its retribution ceases at the level of the Brahmakāyika or Brahmapurohita devas,
yet one attains the concentration of loving-kindness (maitrī-samādhi), then the retribution will be that of a Mahābrahmā.
Since its fruit is so superior, its cause must likewise be great.
If one first attains the fundamental concentration and subsequently applies the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*),
the fundamental concentration becomes even more profound.
Furthermore, within the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), he gives rise to the second dhyāna, accomplishing its four factors including internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*).
He also gives rise to the third dhyāna, accomplishing its five factors including bliss (*sukha*).
Moreover, he gives rise to the fourth dhyāna, each of which corresponds with all the various dhyānas.
When the branches and forest are complete, the flavor of the Dharma increases manifold,
as in the previous analogy.
However, the fundamental object of loving-kindness is that others obtain happiness.
Experiencing internal bliss while observing the bliss of others externally—
these characteristics extend up to the third dhyāna.
In the fourth dhyāna, one observes only that others have attained bliss, while internally there is no experience of bliss.
Because it involves the relinquishing of both suffering and pleasure,
this is the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Such is the distinction.
The Buddha sometimes spoke of breaking through attachment as a condition for merit:
the merit of the mind of loving-kindness reaches the Sphere of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), while the merit of the mind of compassion reaches the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
The merit of the mind of joy extends to the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the merit of the mind of equanimity extends to the sphere of nothingness;
yet, the Bodhisattva is always accompanied by loving-kindness and compassion—
what stage could there be that is devoid of loving-kindness and compassion?
When compassion permeates all wholesome states, how could it be limited merely to the third dhyāna? This is but a general statement.
It is likewise if one first gives rise to the fundamental [dhyāna] and subsequently gives rise to the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
However, all of these were dark realizations that have now vanished;
some were not lost internally but were lost externally, and so forth.
If one relies on the "special excellence" (*viśeṣa*) or "clear illumination" (*āloka*) to develop the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*):
The meditative concentration that serves as the basis is itself one extreme;
the compassion that arises in dependence upon it does not overlap with it.
Since this concentration possesses both contemplation and wisdom, the concentration of compassion is likewise not obscured.
The flavor of the five-limbed dharma is twice as superior as that of the fundamental [dhyāna].
Alternatively, through the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), one may give rise to particularly superior supernormal powers and clear insights (*abhijñā-vidyā*).
This concentration of loving-kindness likewise does not obscure the flavor of dhyāna, and its flavor is profound.
Alternatively, one may develop the minor or major stages of the impurity meditation through the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).

If one perceives sentient beings as having a disintegrating nature through this impurity meditation, then there would be no sentient beings to serve as an object of focus; for whom, then, could this bliss be attained?
Although there is no pleasure within the outflows (*āsrava*) of sentient beings, there is the pleasure of *nirvāṇa*.
This is the loving-kindness that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*). Question:
Loving-kindness takes sentient beings as its object and is characterized by purity and freedom from ill will;
it apprehends their favorable aspects.
Impurity-contemplation, however, breaks down the perception of sentient beings.
Regarding the question of how these unwholesome signs arise:
the answer is that there is no harm in this either.

Just as seeing the impure does not prevent one from also seeing a pure person who is handsome and well-dressed, so too the arising of the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) does not prevent [the perception of] the impure; furthermore,
this concentration of loving-kindness can also adorn the stages of liberation (*vimokṣa*) and so forth.
It causes merit to become doubly profound and superior to that produced by a single [unwholesome] thought;
or rather, they cause one another to arise, and so forth.
The remaining three immeasurable minds likewise cause one another to arise.

This can be understood by analogy with the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). If the four immeasurables arise in conjunction with the fundamental [dhyānas], they constitute the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*).
If they arise in conjunction with the special excellence (*viśeṣa*) or the supernormal clarity (*vidyā*), they constitute both the outflow-tainted and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The attachment to impurity immediately becomes untainted;
this is because the causal conditions differ,
as do the depths of the meditative concentrations on loving-kindness and so forth.
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of kinds beyond description.
For example, within the Desire Realm, the four great elements produce various kinds of earth—
blue, yellow, red, white, high, and low— which in turn produce various kinds of trees, grasses, and fruits.
Whether bitter, sweet, pungent, sour, medicinal, toxic, fragrant, or foul,
[these factors] create various kinds of persons—
handsome or ugly, intelligent or dull-witted, wealthy or poor, virtuous or evil.
He fashioned various birds and beasts with fur and horns, flying and crawling;
their infinite species and grades were distinct and unmixed.
Each according to their own nature and capacity, as is within their power:
just as a person of meager merit relies solely on millet and wild grain,
having no faith that sugarcane or grapes exist.
The pure dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise; they transform the various flavors of the collection of branches, blending with one another yet remaining unmixed.
This continues until the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) become even more vast and expansive.
Why is this? Because sentient beings are immeasurable, the thought of their attaining happiness is likewise immeasurable.
Because all phenomena are immeasurable, the attachment to phenomena and the arising of their branches and flavors are also immeasurable.
Countless sentient beings possess meager merit and do not believe in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Even if they believe in a single teaching, they do not believe in immeasurable merit.
They are like those on the left side of a mountain who do not recognize rare delicacies, or like a frog in a well who denies the existence of the Sea God (*Sāgara*).
This is truly to be pitied.
Those who are able to believe understand that the realm of the sages is inconceivable;
they do not give rise to slander, and so forth.
8. Clarifying the arising through causes and conditions:
When a practitioner has achieved great merit and virtue, the Buddhas bestow upon them meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and samādhi.
Or, due to past habitual tendencies, the causal conditions may be fixed to arise either before or after [the present moment],
and so forth; while sitting,
one suddenly contemplates the object upon which the mind is focused.

Whether taking a wholesome mind as its object or an unwholesome mind as its object, the subjective faculty that perceives and the objective sphere that is perceived constitute the "existence" (bhava) link.
This existence contains the fruit; this existence arises from grasping (upādāna).
It is by means of the mind grasping at good and evil that existence arises;
if one does not grasp, such existence would not exist.
Thus, one knows that existence is born from grasping.
Furthermore, one knows that grasping arises from craving;
because of craving, there is grasping.
For example, if one craves a beautiful form at the time of death, one grasps it; if one does not crave it, then one does not grasp it.
Craving arises from feeling;
because one experiences what is wholesome or unwholesome, craving is produced. If there were no experiencing, craving would not arise.
Furthermore, one observes that feeling depends upon contact.
Because the six sense objects come into contact with the six sense faculties, sensation arises;
without contact, there is no sensation.
As the Sūtra says:
The six types of contact (ṣaḍ-sparśa) are the conditions for the arising of all sensations (vedanā); thus, sensation depends upon contact.
Furthermore, one knows that contact arises from the various sense-gates (āyatana).
If the six consciousnesses do not preside over the six sense faculties, one cannot engage with the various objects to produce contact (*sparśa*).
Contact arises from engagement (*āyatana*), and engagement arises from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); if there were only form, that form could not experience contact, just like a dead person.
If there were only names, even those names would lack contact (*spraṣṭavya*), like a person who is blind or deaf.
Because form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) combine, there is contact.
Form is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The mind consists of the four aggregates.
The discernment of this form is called the aggregate of consciousness;
the experiencing of this form is called the aggregate of sensation.
The arising of craving and aversion within formations is called the two aggregates of name-and-formation (*nāma-rūpa*).
Because the five aggregates are complete, there is sensation and contact;
one should know that contact arises from name-and-formation.
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) begins with the consciousness that first enters the womb;
this initial entry into the womb is called the kalala.
At this stage, it already possesses three factors.
First is vitality (*āyus*), second is warmth (*uṣman*), and third is consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Among these, that which has retributive wind as its basis and is called "wind" is vitality;
that the semen and blood do not become foul-smelling or putrid is warmth.
Among these, mind and intention are called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because consciousness takes hold of the womb, there arise [stages such as] congealed butter and thin curd;
when the six vesicles expand, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) come together.
One should know that name-and-form do not arise apart from consciousness;
consciousness arises from karmic formations.
These are the wholesome karmas of having observed the five precepts in the past.
Karma causes one to receive name-and-form among human beings;
the evil karma of violating the five precepts in the past causes one to receive retribution in the three miserable realms.
Therefore, it is known that consciousness arises from karma, and karma is itself volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Volitional formations arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), delusion, and craving;
through the performance of various formations, consciousness flows on.
From the past it has come to the present; from the present, with craving and grasping as conditions, there is becoming (*bhava*).
This becoming contains the fruit and summons future birth and death.
The causes and conditions of the three periods of time are empty and without a master.
When the wisdom of contemplation arises through such reflection,
the false conceptualizations of a self and persons are immediately shattered;
the concentrated mind becomes tranquil, proceeding from the coarse toward the subtle.
From the threshold stage (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm up to the fivefold fundamental dhyāna, the factors of merit arise in succession;
one realizes that causes and conditions are empty and devoid of a master.
These are called the factors of enlightenment.
As they flow through the three periods of time, they mutually depend upon one another;
their clear cognition is without error.
This is called the limb of contemplation (*dhyāna-aṅga*).
Having attained the wisdom of causes and conditions and deeply understood the three periods of time, how could one not feel joyful?
This is called the limb of joy (*prīti-aṅga*).
The concentration that sustains the mind with tranquility, joy, and sublime excellence is called the factor of bliss (*prīti-aṅga*).
The concentrated mind is profoundly still, without objective conditions and without discursive thought.
This is called the factor of single-mindedness.
This samādhi, which has these as its causes and conditions, is of the nature of wisdom.
Because this wisdom is luminous, it immediately gives rise to the fundamental [samādhi].
Alternatively, when the root and its causal conditions are in harmony,
the flavor of the Dharma is pure and thick, differing from the five factors arising in isolation.
This samādhi also has both hidden and non-hidden aspects.
If one’s inner mind merely understands the law of dependent origination and does not give rise to the inversion of a self,
it is simply in correspondence with the root; yet,
to possess such understanding while remaining in darkness is called "obscuration."
When this samādhi arises, the mind becomes clear and pure;
one perceives the kalala, the five bubbles, and the expansion [of the embryo], as well as the places of birth and dwelling,
and one also sees the good and evil deeds performed through karma, including their beauty and ugliness.
One also clearly perceives the matters of birth and death in the future; thus, the three periods of time are distinct.
This is called the mark of non-obscuration.
Both of these possess the ten dharmas of emptiness and clarity, which are fully accomplished.
This is called the fundamental arising through causes and conditions.
Even up to the *viśeṣa*, *abhijñā*, *vidyā*, and *vimokṣa*— whether they are obscured or unobscured—
their arising through causes and conditions is likewise the same.
If one generates the causal conditions based on the root [concentration],
one suddenly contemplates within meditative absorption that all root concentrations are produced by causes and conditions.
That which is accomplished and that which accomplishes are precisely existence.
This coarse and subtle abiding encompasses the realms of the Yama, Tushita, and other heavens.
Where there is birth, there must be death.
The realm of desire is also existentially conditioned by causes and conditions.
Where there is existence, there is the fruit that entails rebirth among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations.
Where there is birth, there is death.
The preparatory concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) is also an existence by way of causes and conditions.
Since it is an existence, it must contain its fruit; thus, one should experience the existence of the Māra-heaven.
Being associated with the first dhyāna, it already contains that existence.
This applies even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
All such states arise due to grasping; one grasps the characteristics of the first dhyāna as described previously in the twenty-five preparatory methods (*pūrvayoga*).
One grasps at various objects of hope by apprehending their characteristics;
thus, one knows that grasping arises from clinging, and clinging in turn arises from craving.
This is because, upon hearing others describe the merits of the first dhyāna, one gives rise to a relish for it.
Furthermore, one knows that this craving arises from feeling;
for by hearing of another's virtues, one experiences them and thereby gives rise to craving.
Furthermore, one knows that this feeling arises through the sense-bases (*āyatana*), for the sense-bases are themselves the faculties (*indriya*);
without the faculties and sense-bases, there is no feeling.
Moreover, feeling exists because of contact with objects (*viṣaya-sparśa*); thus, there is the sense-base-contact, which arises from name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Through the conjunction of the five aggregates, contact arises.
Name-and-form proceeds from the initial consciousness;
these three factors come together through karma to receive a body.
Karma, arising from ignorance, leads to birth, consciousness, and so forth, up to old age and death.
From the highest realm of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception down to the coarse abodes of existence,
one clearly understands each of these twelve links of dependent origination.
This applies even up to the *viśeṣa*, *abhijñā*, and *vidyā* stages, which all arise from the fundamental cause;
this can be understood by analogy, and so forth.
Since this contemplation destroys the notion of a self, it is identical in intent to the preliminary method (*upāya*) for destroying the self within the [Dhātu] section.
It is merely based on the *Dhyāna-sūtra* that the name "samādhi of the causal conditions" (*pratītyasamutpāda-samādhi*) is received.
Although it is of the nature of wisdom when sought through the three periods of time, it is still called "stilling the mind.
The mind attains a state of stillness and abiding, like a sealed chamber without wind.
One may practice the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).

Only when the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness is perfected is it called "wisdom derived from hearing" (śrutamayī-prajñā). Wisdom derived from hearing is indeed contemplation based on principle (li-guan).
As Purna’s realization states:
"I have understood; I already know. How do you know?
If one knows that ignorance does not give rise to grasping for existence."
This refers to the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā).
This contemplation of causes and conditions lacks such power prior to the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna);
therefore, it belongs to the contemplation of phenomena (vastu-vipaśyanā).
This gate of causes and conditions varies according to the capacities of beings.
The *Ratnavyūha* clarifies ten kinds of great assemblies that clarify the retribution of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*),
whereas most masters transmit [the teaching of] the three periods of time.
Nāgārjuna composed the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, beginning with the "Examination of Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*).
The masters [of other schools] claimed that this did not encompass all phenomena and was not established as the primary tenet [of the Madhyamaka],
but was merely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The exhaustion of causes and conditions through their deconstruction is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Therefore, the two truths constitute the core tenet [of this teaching].
Now, it is asked: which category is not conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) such that all are exhausted through deconstruction?
This is the general approach and not a specific intent.
At the beginning of the treatise, the causes and conditions are examined in a general manner;
subsequently, the branches of craving and grasping are refuted individually within the section on the defiled categories.
The sixth chapter distinguishes the afflictions to refute the factors of suffering;
even down to the final two chapters, which separately present the śrāvaka’s contemplation of dependent origination,
the general and specific intentions all consist in contemplating dependent origination.
Is it not because they take causal conditions as their fundamental tenet?
The Northern Master adopts the salvific arguments from the latter chapter,
taking the six causes and four conditions as his fundamental tenet.
This is precisely the causal condition for arising and ceasing.
The intent of the final two chapters is not the primary tenet of this treatise;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the faculties of sentient beings became increasingly dull.
Those who grasp at the fixed characteristics of the causal conditions of dependent origination fail to understand the Buddha’s intent;
therefore, this treatise is composed to clarify the gate of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination.
Now that the dharma of dependent origination has been introduced, I shall explain *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* by means of it.
For example, as stated in the "Ten Intentions" and so forth:
regarding the realm of conceptual deliberation,
it refers to the performance of black karma and various unwholesome deeds within the mind of past ignorance.
One forms the realms of the three miserable destinies;
by performing various white karmas and immovable karmas,
one forms the realms of the three wholesome destinies.
If one transforms ignorance into the wisdom that perceives arising and ceasing,
it is called the contemplation of inferior wisdom, through which one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.
If one transforms contaminated activities into practices that assist the supramundane path, [it is called the contemplation of superior wisdom].
The seven types of learners (*śaikṣa*), whose residual karma is not yet exhausted, are still born into the wholesome realms.
If there were no unconditioned activity (*anāsrava-karman*) and attachment to the true reality (*satya-lobha*) of those beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*),
[the afflictions] would merely combine with fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Being born in the land of skillful means and receiving name-and-form therein,
one gives rise to grasping and existence through craving and aversion;
this is the realm of the śrāvakas.
If one reverses ignorance into the clarity of non-arising and non-ceasing, then through this middle-grade wisdom, one attains the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha.
As stated in the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*: [text follows].
Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination as being like a dream, an illusion, or a plantain tree constitutes the path of the pratyekabuddha;
this is the intended meaning.
It involves transforming tainted states of existence into untainted factors that assist the path.
Whether the karma of their fetters is exhausted or not is the same as previously described;
this constitutes the realm of the pratyekabuddha.
If they transform ignorance into *prajñā* and transform unwholesome conduct into the five perfections, [they become Buddhas].
Because those who have not yet awakened to the truth still possess the twelve links of dependent origination within the realm [of ignorance],
this is the realm of the six perfections.
If one transforms ignorance into the wisdom of emptiness and transforms volitional formations into the six perfections, [this is the transformation].

Volitional formations and existence are the conditional cause of Buddha-nature;

The path of suffering is the transformation of birth-and-death; the body of birth-and-death is itself the Dharma-body. Afflictions are the dharma of darkness; transforming ignorance into clarity.

When the fruit is attained through cultivation, it is neither vertical nor horizontal,
like the worldly letter *i*;

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

If one has not yet severed the five grades of delusions, one is a fellow student.
Those with the iron wheel-turner’s mark have long been parted from the ocean of suffering and are equal to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

As the *Śāstra* says:
The faculties of those of the Two Vehicles who receive the Dharma-nature body are dull and dark,

If one follows the Separate or Perfect [Teachings], one can shatter ignorance and directly open the path of suffering— the Dharma as it truly is.

directly within the process of conditioned existence, one fulfills all practices and thereby realizes the environment and its inhabitants without any obstruction.

Question:
The *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states:
The dharmas conditioned by causes are in reality without arising.
If one claims they do arise, does this occur within a single mind or within a plurality of minds?
One might also say that it exists within a single thought-moment.
Answer: The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
Within one there are immeasurables; within the immeasurable there is one.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All dharmas tend toward ignorance; they do not transcend this tendency."
Up to and including the fact that all phenomena tend toward old age and death—
now, in stating that a single mind is fully endowed with the twelve links of dependent origination,
what fault could there be?
Furthermore, as for the term "a single thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa),
it is not like the single, fixed characteristic of oneness or difference grasped by worldly people;
rather, it is spoken of as "one" precisely because it is neither one nor different.
For example, just as when the mind is overwhelmed by phenomena, one dreams of immeasurable worldly affairs within a single thought-moment—
as described in detail in the *Lotus Sūtra*—
so it is for one who has truly resolved their mind toward Bodhi.
If one gives rise to compassionate vows based on the twelve links of dependent origination— such as those involving arising and ceasing, or non-arising and non-ceasing, and so forth—
this is not the true and ultimate reality.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra states that "the demon of the bodhicitta" refers to this very point.
If one relies on the inconceivable twelve links of dependent origination to give rise to compassion,
one will universally deliver all beings.
This is called the true and correct [removal].
There are two ways of uprooting suffering.
First, uprooting the five kinds of causal suffering consisting of ignorance, craving, grasping, and formations within the ten dharma realms.
Second, one eradicates the seven kinds of resultant suffering consisting of consciousness, name-and-form, and so forth within the ten dharma-realms.
Compassion that bestows happiness is likewise:
it means bestowing upon the ten dharma-realms the wisdom, conduct, and right path that arise from contemplating ignorance, craving, and grasping.
The transformation of practice results in perfected practice that assists the path;
this is called the cause for bestowing happiness.
One contemplates that the ten realms, name-and-form, and the seven branches are all of the nature of peace and bliss.
That is, Great Nirvana cannot be extinguished again;
it is named the fruit of bliss.
Based on these four meanings, one gives rise to the Four Great Vows.
To cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over—
crossing over the suffering of the sevenfold cycle of birth and death within the ten realms;
to cause those who have not yet attained liberation to attain liberation.
One understands the accumulation of the five branches— ignorance, craving, grasping, formations, and becoming— within the ten realms;
one brings those who have not yet attained peace to peace,
establishing them in the primary and auxiliary paths regarding ignorance, craving, grasping, formations, and becoming within the ten realms.
It is said that for those who have not yet attained *nirvāṇa*, it brings about the peace and bliss of *nirvāṇa* through the seven factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth.
Regarding "skillful settling of the mind" (*śayanasthiti-kuśala*): [text continues].
Skillfully observing that the seven factors, such as consciousness within the ten realms, are themselves the dharma-nature (dharmatā),

and not giving rise to ignorance, craving, grasping, the eight inversions, or delusions, is called "observing the cessation of the various inversions of the ten dharma-realms, such as formations and existence."
Therefore, it is called "stopping," and so forth.
As for "the universal destruction of dharmas":
it horizontally destroys the ten realms and the twelve links of dependent origination, showing that they are all, in their entirety, a single thought-moment.
In a single thought-moment, there is no self, no other, no commonality, and no lack of cause;
one should know that the ten realms are entirely without arising.
Vertically, by shattering the practices of the ten realms, the afflictions of views and thoughts, the dust-like and sand-like [afflictions], and the ignorance of non-cognition do not arise.
Up to the forty-second category, the non-arising of non-arising is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
This is what is meant by "skillfully knowing the open and the obstructed."
Thoroughly comprehending the true nature of causes and conditions is called "penetration.
Arising views, afflictions, and attachments constitutes an obstruction;
sinking into the truth itself is non-penetration. Thoroughly comprehending the phenomena of causes and conditions is non-obstruction.
To give rise to attachment to dharmas within the three paths constitutes an obstruction;
to penetrate the principle within causes and conditions is called penetration.
If, at each successive stage, one gives rise to ignorance, craving, grasping, formations, and becoming, this constitutes a failure.
If, in each successive stage, one possesses wisdom, it is called "attainment" (*prāpti*);
alternatively, it refers directly to the fourfold application regarding the suffering and origin [of the aggregates],
while the fourfold path and cessation serve as the means of penetration.

Alternatively, because one directly addresses the three provisional designations (trividha-prajñapti), this serves as the "obstruction" (saṃvara); by refuting the non-arising of these three provisional designations, it becomes the "penetration" (vyutthāna).
Just as it is with the pervasive afflictions (kleśa), so it is with the specific afflictions (paryavasthāna) as well.
Alternatively, one may directly address the four views by giving rise to the ten proclivities as obstructions;
then, by breaking through these views, they become passages, and so forth.
This is for those who skillfully cultivate the factors of enlightenment.
If discussed generally within the context of the causes and conditions of the ten realms, all phenomena of form (*rūpa*) are termed "body" (*kāya*);
all phenomena of sensation (*vedanā*) are termed "feeling" (*vedanā*);
and all phenomena of consciousness (*vijñāna*) are termed "mind" (*citta*).
All formations of perception are termed "dharmas.
To speak of them specifically,
one takes up "form" from within the branch of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Among the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), five bases are taken;
among the contacts (*sparśa*), five contacts and five feelings (*vedanā*) are taken;
and from each of the links of birth and death (*jāti* and *jarāmaraṇa*), the portion consisting of form (*rūpa*) is taken.
All are subsumed under the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).
Within the factors of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the portion of consciousness (vijñāna) is taken;
within the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), the mental base (manāyatana) is taken.
The portions of consciousness taken from each of the members of birth and death are all subsumed under the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*).
From among the members of ignorance, formations, and name-and-form, one takes perception and mental formations.
Within the member of contact (*sparśa*), one takes up the contact with mental objects (*dharmasparśa*).
Within the members of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), and birth (*jāti*), one takes up perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
Within the member of death (*maraṇa*), one likewise takes up perception and mental formations.
All are subsumed under the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). At other times,
it is said that ignorance (*avidyā*) is past craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving is the defilement of the five aggregates.
If discussed in terms of the present, it is subsumed under the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) within the category of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The practice of the Dharma is subsumed under [the aggregate of] formations; consciousness is subsumed under mind;
and name-and-form is subsumed under both body and mind.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are conditioned by the six objects (ṣaḍviṣaya).
The objects are subsumed under the category of dharmas; the sense bases are subsumed under the category of the body.
Contact is subsumed under mental objects;
feeling is, in turn, subsumed under feeling;
craving defiles both body and mind and is thus subsumed under both.
It is comprised by the dharma;
it is comprised by conditioned activity.
That this form arises is birth; that this form ceases is death; thus it is comprised by the dharma.
Question:

Some teachers say that birth and death are all formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and should therefore be subsumed under the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*) alone.
Why, then, are they said to be included within all three applications of mindfulness?
Answer: The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:
"When these five aggregates cease, those five aggregates arise in succession."
Just as when a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal is destroyed while the impression is formed,
one knows that the phenomena of birth and death do not exist apart from the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Thus it can be said, and so forth.
If one can simultaneously illuminate both defilement and purity regarding all forms— whether general or specific, whether caused by conditions or not—
this is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Contemplating all causes and conditions, as well as the general and specific aspects of sensation—
neither suffering nor pleasure, while simultaneously illuminating both suffering and pleasure—
is called the foundation of mindfulness of sensation.
Contemplating all causes and conditions through both their general and specific aspects of mind and consciousness—
neither eternal nor impermanent, but observing both eternity and impermanence simultaneously—
is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
Contemplating the general and specific characteristics of all causes and conditions within perception and mental formations,
neither as self nor as non-self, but illuminating both self and non-self simultaneously—
this is the application of mindfulness to dharmas.
These four [realizations] are able to destroy the eight kinds of perversions within the twelve links of dependent origination.
These eight perversions transform into the four types of withering and the four types of flourishing;
they are also the intermediate state that is neither withering nor flourishing.
Entering into nirvana is the seeing of the Buddha-nature.
Diligently contemplating these four is called right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*).
Up to the eightfold path, it is as explained previously.
Contemplating the fundamental [nature], there are not four propositions;
that which is neither arising nor ceasing is ultimate emptiness.
This emptiness encompasses the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
The eighteen emptinesses are in fact but a single emptiness.
The Vaipulya scriptures state:
"Small emptiness and great emptiness both return to the one emptiness."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"First, solitary emptiness;
this is called the gate of liberation through emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*)."
All enter this emptiness and do not grasp at the four characteristics of the dharma-nature.
They do not accept or cling to it;
they do not dwell upon it or discriminate between the new and the old, the internal and the external, and so forth.
If the mind has no dependence,
one sees the true Buddha-nature through non-seeing;
by not abiding in any phenomena, one dwells in great nirvāṇa.
This is called the liberation door of signlessness.
This Great Nirvāṇa is neither cultivated nor created;
because it is not self, it is without cause.
It is not due to another, thus it is not a condition;
it is not shared, thus it is not a conjunction;
it is not without cause, thus it is not a separation.
The gate of liberation called "non-cultivation and non-attainment" is the counteractive aid to the path.
Whereas the preceding factors of enlightenment directly take principle as their object, [this gate] functions as their antidote.

Furthermore, there are formations (*saṃskāra*) and objects (*vastu*) that are unwholesome and assist in obscuring rational wisdom.
Just as when one is outnumbered by many thieves, one must apply diligent cultivation.

if there is the arising of the practice of laziness...

the qualities of its constituent branches are produced;
if existence arises as the practice of delusion, [the same occurs].
Transforming [the mind] into the practice of awakening to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and conditioned existence,

one should contemplate and practice these as previously described.
Furthermore, regarding the Buddha’s majestic deportment:
his sitting at the site of enlightenment, his turning of the wheel of Dharma,
and his entry into nirvana are all based upon the twelve links of dependent origination.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"If one can deeply contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination,
this is itself sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)."
There are four types of sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
If one contemplates the ultimate arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination,
this is the site where the Buddha of the Tripitaka sat upon a wooden tree and a grass seat at the place of enlightenment.
If one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being ultimately empty, this is the ultimate [realization] of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) Buddha;
he sits at the site of enlightenment upon a throne of celestial raiment beneath trees of the seven precious gems.
If one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being ultimately provisional designations, this is the ultimate [realization] of the Shared Teaching Buddha.
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the Śākyamuni Buddha sits upon a jeweled throne at the site of enlightenment;
if one contemplates the ultimate within the twelve links of dependent origination,
this is the Vairocana Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) sitting at the site of enlightenment with empty space as his throne.
One should know that the great and small *maṇḍalas* do not transcend the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Furthermore, all Buddhas turn the wheel of Dharma by means of this very contemplation.

this is also called "provisional designation" and is also called the meaning of the "Middle Way."

whereas, in the Vaipulya scriptures consisting of the twelve divisions,
he taught that the arising and ceasing of the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves emptiness, themselves provisionality, and themselves the Middle Way.

whereas the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* explains the twelve links of dependent origination as being the Middle—
thereby setting aside the three skillful means.

just as milk possesses the nature of clarified butter (ghṛta).

they are all skillful distinctions based upon the twelve links of dependent origination, manifested as guidance according to the capacities of sentient beings.

It is because, initially, for disciples of dull faculties...

They immediately awaken to the Buddha-nature and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is the secret intent.
This is the manner in which the Wheel of Dharma is turned within the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
Furthermore, all Buddhas attain parinirvāṇa through this very contemplation.

Regarding the exhaustion of both afflictions and their habitual tendencies:

This is the *nirvāṇa* of permanence, bliss, self, and purity of the Buddha according to the Distinct Teaching (*piehiao*).
In terms of the twelve links of dependent origination,
the three paths are themselves the three Buddha-natures,
and likewise the three nirvāṇas.
Nirvāṇa is named the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas;
it is the nirvāṇa of four virtues belonging to the Vairocana Buddha of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

There are four kinds,

As for the successive stages of consciousness:
The lightness or gravity of the three evil realms is entirely due to ignorance, unwholesome conduct, and craving and grasping.

this involves six stages of practice with varying levels of height.

Within a single person and a single thought-moment, the twelve links of dependent origination are fully present.

for space has neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion.

"Emptiness is called the Mahāyāna;

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"This vehicle neither moves nor emerges.
